newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's biggest holding firm says it's solvent.
newsitem.headline: Albania's biggest holding firm says it's solvent.

text.p: Vehbi Alimucaj, founder of the biggest investment holding firm in Albania, said on Monday angry investors should "roll up their sleeves and get back to work" instead of protesting and burning down buildings.
His Vefa company, a household name in Albania, froze the deposits of its 80,000 investors after five fraudulent pyramid investment schemes went bust last month and caused a panic.
Alimucaj told Reuters in an interview that his investors had nothing to fear and would get back their deposits in three or four months after a climate of insecurity had passed.
"We are prepared and proceeding with a definite timetable for paying this capital," he said. Meanwhile, he said, Vefa had cash and was making interest payments to 2,000 to 3,000 people a day.

Seated at his cluttered desk at Vefa's Tirana headquarters, he rejected comparisons between his company, which boasts 240 different businesses, and the get-rich-quick investment schemes which collapsed.
Referring to his Sunday appeal on his EuroVefa television channel, Alimucaj said: "After my appearance many ill-wishers said Vefa had gone bankrupt. Let me assure you Vefa is very sound."
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has been rocked by riots and protests for a month, with furious investors demanding that the government reimburse them for losses and then resign.
Officials estimate $1 billion to $2 billion were invested in the failed schemes and since then all eyes have been on Vefa and three other big holding companies which froze client deposits.
Alimucaj said Vefa had 27 outlets around Albania and assets of $500 to $600 million in businesses from tourism, poultry and beer production to a sausage factory and 30,000 sheep.
"Vefa is the ABC of capitalism in Albania. We have done many kinds of investments over the past five years," he said.

Albania emerged from 45 years of isolationism and Stalinism only in 1990. President Sali Berisha has blamed a naive public for succumbing to the lure of interest rates of 60 percent a month and pumping millions of dollars into fraudulent schemes.
Alimucaj said many Albanians had become used to a soft life over the past five years, living off pyramid scheme interest payments and remittances from children working abroad.

"Have they forgotten already when they received a kilo of meat a month and a kilo of cheese every six weeks? Or getting a black and white television took three years and meant asking a manager 1,000 times?," he asked.
Alimucaj said he began with nothing, working in a warehouse and then buying and selling old clothes. Only investment would ensure growth and jobs, he said.

"Many Albanians have money at home but are afraid now to put it in investment companies or state banks. People should circulate money. It would be in the best interest of the nation to invest this money and create jobs," he added.
Asked what he would say to thousands of people who lost their life savings in the pyramid schemes, he said: "I would appeal to them to roll up their sleeves and get back to work."
He added: "Big money cannot come from dreaming and playing billiards and pool and cards all day or sitting around drinking coffee in cafes."
While he spoke inside his headquarters, a flashy red-brick house which stages nightly light-shows, beefy bodyguards herded anxious investors away from the buildings' iron gates.
The guards were most upset when investors tried to talk to foreign reporters, fearing the crowd of people could trigger a spontaneous demonstration -- taboo in Tirana.
One woman, Mimosa, carried her sleeping 14-month-old baby, Angela, and said she had sold her apartment to invest in two fraudulent funds and in Vefa.
She put $15,000 in the Gypsy-run Sude fund and $5,000 in the Populli fund -- which both went bust -- and $5,000 in Vefa, which had frozen its accounts.
"I wish my daughter had never been born. How will we take care of her?" she wept. Bodyguards pushed her away quickly.
Alimucaj said such distraught investors had nothing to fear from Vefa and would get their money back. But he said there was no question of selling assets to pay investors their capital.

"If we sold our assets and paid them, I would have $300 million left and could sit around all day drinking coffee in cafes like protesters. But I am committed to capitalism and to developing my country," he said.
